That error usually means the Docker CLI is still using the old Docker Desktop socket (a leftover docker context or a DOCKER_HOST export in your shell profile) rather than OrbStack's. Switching the context to OrbStack's should fix it without touching the compose file.
Action: run `docker context ls` and `echo $DOCKER_HOST` to see what's pointing at the old socket, then switch to the orbstack context and retry `docker compose up`.

`as const` changes the inferred type of a value: it makes it deeply readonly and narrows literals (`['a','b'] as const` becomes `readonly ['a','b']`). `satisfies` checks a value against a type without changing its inferred type, so you get validation and keep the narrow literals (`const x = {...} satisfies Config`). Use `as const` to freeze/narrow, `satisfies` to type-check without widening, and they combine fine as `{...} as const satisfies Config`.
Action: none needed; I can show a small example in the repo if that would help.

`docker compose up -d` creates (or recreates if config/image changed) the containers, networks and volumes and starts them in the background. `docker compose start` only starts containers that already exist and were stopped; it won't create anything or pick up compose file changes. So use `up -d` normally and `start` just to resume stopped containers.

The common thread is TS1484: with `verbatimModuleSyntax` enabled, anything that is only a type must be imported with `import type { X }` (or an inline `type` modifier like `import { type X }`). The errors are all type-only imports (ClientRow, Invoice, ColumnDef, FastifyPluginAsync and so on) written as regular imports. It's mechanical to fix.
Action: confirm the tsconfig setting, then use the linter's auto-fix for type-only imports if the repo's linter has one, otherwise apply `import type` edits, and re-run typecheck across web and api.

Sums coming back as strings is typical when Postgres returns SUM over integer/bigint/numeric columns as a string via the driver. I'd cast in the query or convert at the route boundary, so the JSON has real numbers; I'll check the column types first so I don't lose precision.
Action: open apps/api/src/routes/stats.ts, convert the sums to numbers (SQL cast or `Number()` in the mapping), and add or update a test asserting the response types.

A Deployment runs interchangeable pods: any pod can be replaced or scaled freely, with random names and typically shared or no storage. A StatefulSet gives each pod a stable identity (ordinal name, stable DNS via a headless Service), ordered start/stop and its own persistent volume per pod. Pick a StatefulSet for things like databases, Kafka or Zookeeper, where each replica needs stable identity and its own data.
Action: none needed; I'll check on the trailmix tests.

Next middleware runs on the edge runtime by default because it runs before routing and caching on every matched request, so it needs to be fast and lightweight and deployable close to users. That limits it to Web APIs, with no Node-only modules. Newer Next versions allow opting into the Node.js runtime for middleware, depending on version.
Action: check the Next version in apps/web, and tell you whether the Node runtime option is available for our middleware.ts (Clerk's) before suggesting anything.

AsyncLocalStorage carries context (like a request id or user) through async calls without passing it as a parameter, which is the typical use for request context and log correlation. It has a small overhead, and recent Node versions have reduced it, so it's generally fine for per-request context but I wouldn't measure by guesswork.
Action: none needed; if you want, I can wire the request id into the logger and Sentry via it after the tests finish.
